pr.title: mitigate MSVC alignment issue on x86-32
pr.description:
This implements mitigation for https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/112480 by stopping to emit `align` attributes on loads and function arguments when building for a win32 MSVC target. MSVC is known to not properly align `u64` and similar types, and claiming to LLVM that everything is properly aligned increases the chance that this will cause problems.

Of course, the misalignment is still a bug, but we can't fix that bug, only MSVC can.

Also add an errata note to the platform support page warning users about this known problem.

try-job: `i686-msvc*`
pr.author: RalfJung

analysis.summary: On 32-bit x86 Windows, MSVC fails to align u64/i64 and other >4-byte-aligned types reliably. Historically CheckAlignment was simply disabled for i686-pc-windows-msvc, and alignment was otherwise treated as fully reliable. The fix introduces Target::max_reliable_alignment() (4 bytes for is_like_windows && arch=="x86", otherwise Align::MAX), weakens CheckAlignment's alignment mask to the reliable-alignment mask instead of skipping the pass, and clamps align annotations used by LLVM loads/stores and function-argument pointee alignment.
analysis.originalLogic: CheckAlignment::is_enabled returned false for i686-pc-windows-msvc due to "FIXME(#112480) MSVC and rustc disagree on minimum stack alignment on x86 Windows", falling back to `sess.ub_checks()`. When enabled, insert_alignment_check builds an alignment mask from the place's required alignment and inserts a MIR check that the pointer's low bits are zero. Separately, codegen load/store used the requested `align` directly, and ABI construction used `attrs.pointee_align = Some(pointee.align)`, both asserting full requested alignment to LLVM.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historically incorrect target-specific behavior was to suppress the CheckAlignment pass entirely on i686-pc-windows-msvc (an early `return false`), and to keep asserting full requested alignment to LLVM. A naive alternative would be to remove that disable and run the unmodified check, which would flag the platform's own 4-byte-only alignment as Rust UB. The corrected transformation keeps the pass enabled but further limits the alignment mask by ANDing it with the mask for the highest reliable alignment, e.g. required mask 7 becomes 3 on win32 x86, and clamps load/store/pointee alignment with `align.min(max_reliable_alignment())`.
analysis.inputDomain: MIR containing alignment checks for pointer dereferences/casts, and codegen load/store and ABI argument attributes carrying requested alignment. Program pairs should differ only in the target-dependent alignment-mask clamping: same MIR/IR with required alignment > 4, compiled for a target whose max_reliable_alignment is 4 (32-bit x86 Windows) versus one where it is Align::MAX. For CheckAlignment tests, ub_checks must be enabled.
analysis.trigger: Triggered when alignment is requested on 32-bit x86 Windows: `self.is_like_windows && self.arch == "x86"` yields max_reliable_alignment 4. In CheckAlignment, the mask-clamping branch runs when `max_align < Align::MAX`; load/store and pointee-align clamps change behavior only when the requested alignment exceeds the target's reliable alignment.
preconditions: CheckAlignment must be enabled, which requires `sess.ub_checks()`; the old target-based early return for i686-pc-windows-msvc was removed.
The target must report a max_reliable_alignment below Align::MAX; source implementation returns 4 when target `is_like_windows && self.arch == "x86"`, for both MSVC and GNU Windows x86 targets.
The alignment in question must exceed the reliable alignment (e.g. an 8-byte-aligned u64) for clamping to be observable.
For load/store codegen, `flags.contains(MemFlags::UNALIGNED)` still forces alignment 1 after the min operation.
pitfalls: Do not treat the fix as repairing MSVC: the PR says `Every target that returns less than Align::MAX here is still has a soundness bug.`

Suppressing the stronger part of the alignment check means real misalignment that exceeds reliable alignment is no longer detected; the PR states that the change would detect this unsoundness via alignment checks that are suppressed.

Do not limit the mitigation to the MSVC target tuple only: max_reliable_alignment uses `is_like_windows && self.arch == "x86"`, and regression codegen tests ignore both i686-pc-windows-msvc and i686-pc-windows-gnu.
The alignment-mask AND must use `max_align.bytes() - 1` as the mask; using the alignment value itself rather than its mask is wrong for bitwise-AND checking.
Clamping applies to both loads and stores; dropping the clamp on stores or overwriting the UNALIGNED alignment-1 result would regress the mitigation.
ABI pointee alignment must be clamped with `pointee.align.min(max_reliable_alignment())`, otherwise function-argument attributes still over-promise alignment to LLVM.
analysis.testStrategy: Add target-gated MIR/UB-check tests on i686 Windows x86 that exercise a pointer requiring >4-byte alignment and verify the emitted alignment mask is clamped to the max reliable alignment while the pass is still enabled (unlike the old early return). Add codegen tests showing load/store and argument alignment annotations are capped at 4 on i686 Windows. Inspect existing codegen alignment tests: this PR marks `tests/codegen/align-struct.rs` and `tests/codegen/issues/issue-56927.rs` with `//@ ignore-i686-pc-windows-msvc` and `//@ ignore-i686-pc-windows-gnu`, with the comment `// 32bit MSVC does not align things properly so we suppress high alignment annotations (#112480)`; those ignores are regression-suite accommodations, not proof that the clamping is absent. Verify non-i686/non-Windows targets still receive Align::MAX and unchanged high-alignment annotations. Do not claim compiler execution or reproduction without building.
evidence: FIXME(#112480) MSVC and rustc disagree on minimum stack alignment on x86 Windows
This implements mitigation for https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/112480 by stopping to emit `align` attributes on loads and function arguments when building for a win32 MSVC target.
MSVC is known to not properly align `u64` and similar types, and claiming to LLVM that everything is properly aligned increases the chance that this will cause problems.
// If this target does not have reliable alignment, further limit the mask by anding it with
// the mask for the highest reliable alignment.
Every target that returns less than `Align::MAX` here is still has a soundness bug.
if flags.contains(MemFlags::UNALIGNED) { 1 } else { align.bytes() as c_uint };
// 32bit MSVC does not align things properly so we suppress high alignment annotations (#112480)
